newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS-Asset sales help Paribas to profit.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Asset sales help Paribas to profit.

text.p: French holding company Groupe Paribas returned convincingly to profit last year, reversing a big 1995 loss incurred from writedowns on loss-making investments.
An accelerated programme of asset sales -- aided by a strong French stock market-- plus stronger operating performances at all its business units lifted the company out of the red.

Paribas chairman Andre Levy-Lang on Thursday said the company used 1996 to position itself for continued and consistent growth and added that troubles of 1995 and earlier years would no longer haunt its results.
"The commitments we made at the beginning of 1996 were all respected," Levy-Lang told a news conference.
"We believe Paribas is today in a position to grow and has the elements to recover a dynamic of growth," he added.
Paribas said it earned 4.35 billion francs ($764 million) in 1996 after a four billion franc loss the year before. In 1994, the company earned 1.75 billion francs.
The company's earnings were significantly boosted by a 1.82 billion franc profit at its flagship Banque Paribas unit, which it said had rebuilt its financial resources during 1996.
Paribas shares were up 3.10 francs or 0.78 percent to 398.10 in early afternoon trading, in line with the bourse as a whole.
Paribas said the potential for capital gains on its equity portfolio had increased last year, despite its many asset sales which fulfilled disposal goals originally set for three years.
It said its return on equity (ROE) had risen to 12.1 percent, surpassing its goal of boosting ROE to 10 percent by 1999.
Paribas profits last year could have been higher were it not for 2.5 billion francs of exceptional provisions taken by its Cie Bancaire unit "to eliminate real estate risks".
Paribas also took provisions to cover the cost of transition to a single European currency.
Its 1995 loss, a rare event at the company, was due mostly to a hefty 2.13 billion franc provision to write down the value of its 31 percent stake in diversified conglomerate Cie de Navigation Mixte.

Other 1995 charges included 1.9 billion francs against losses at its Cogedim property development unit and 1.19 billion francs for assets transferred from its Credit du Nord unit, which it has since agreed to sell to French commercial bank Societe Generale.
But since the writedown of its investments, Paribas has taken majority control of Mixte and recorded significant capital gains from selling many of its assets.
The sale of assets held by Mixte allowed it to recoup cash equal to the 8.7 billion franc takeover of Mixte, which was originally financed with debt.
It has also moved to isolate itself from property losses at its various units.
